projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Aaron S. Fox was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Aaron S. Fox. Mr. Fox served in the Marines, and his highest rank was corporal. Aaron served in the Pacific Theater, and he took part in the invasion of Guam at Iwo Jima. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Fox's home in Cuyahoga Falls, Ohio, on March 26, 2003. Aaron was 77 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: I was living in Cleveland, Ohio, in the old ethnic neighborhood off of East 105th Street between Superior and St. Claire Avenue.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you still in high school at the time?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: I was in -- yes, I was in Glenville High School.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yes, I remember sitting in front of a little table bible, Atwater Kent. My mother was there with me, and I remember yelling, "Good" when they announced that we had been attacked, and we were -- we had declared war on Japan. And I remember my mother being quite shocked. She looked at me and said, "Don't say that. Don't say, 'Good." It's not good." But I was glad that we were finally in the war and were going to help out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you feel that way just because you were a young, excitable kid, or did you know the world situation and know that we needed to be in the war?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: I followed it very carefully for a young guy. I watched the progress of the war in Europe, and I had maps with pins in it, and I was very involved, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, after war was declared and before you went into the -- you went in the Marines; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before you went into the Marines, did you do anything for the war effort while you were still in school?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah, I became an air raid warden. There was an elderly gentleman who was the chief warden for that district, and I wanted to do something, so I got a white helmet, and we had air raid drills, and I would go knock on doors and tell them to turn their lights out and so forth. But yeah, that was my war effort, air raid warden.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any air raid scares in Cleveland during that time?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: No, just me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get involved in scrap drives or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah, there were all sorts of things, scrap drives, paper, grease that was collected. Everybody did -- everybody was very much involved in the war effort, at least in that community.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, the grease, this is like bacon grease, etcetera, things like that?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that just to grease machinery, or what was it used for?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: No, I think it was used to make munitions.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Dried it and used it?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were -- when did you graduate from high school?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Well, I didn't graduate.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. When did you leave high school?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: In 19 -- the end of 1943, I was in the 12th grade. I had come from Missouri. We moved here, and somehow I was a grade ahead of where I should have been, and I was always associated with older guys. And the older guys, 18, were being drafted and/or enlisting, mostly being drafted; and all the girls were sending those letters with the lipstick smudges on them, SWAK, and there were all these farewell parties, and I was envious. And I was a year younger -- I was 17 -- but I wanted to start getting those letters and everything else. So I went down, saw the Marine recruiter, and he said, "If you sign up now," he said, "I can guarantee that you're going to go to Dago." And I didn't know what that meant. I said, "What do you mean, Dago?" I thought he meant Italians in the pejorative sense. And he said, "No, San Diego instead of Parris Island," which was a horrible place. So I enlisted and had to fake my mother's signature and told my principal at Glenville High School that I was going to be leaving. I was in -- I still had the 12A to complete, and he was very shocked. I was a fairly good student, and he said, "Well, all you really need to do to get your diploma is complete a course in trigonometry. Take your trig book with you, and if you're able to, study, and then we'll send you an exam. If you pass it, we'll send a diploma to you." So that was my high school ending.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did you finish your high school in the boot camp, or what happened?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: I had the book. When boot camp was over, we came time to be assigned to different advanced training things, infantry, etcetera. One of the officers saw the trig book, and he said, "Did you study that?" And I said, "Yeah." He said, "Well, we'll make you a forward observer." And I didn't know what that meant, but I became a forward observer for artillery, and you had to do a little bit of geometry in your head to figure out the elevations and so on and so forth, and that's how I became a forward observer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you actually go into the Marines?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: It was February -- actually, I went in December of 1943, but I got to boot camp early February, 1944.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any stories from boot camp from your training that you can share?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Everybody's heard the horror stories about boot camp. It was -- it was a dehuman -- human -- how would you say it?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Dehumanizing?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Dehumanizing experience. One of the things I do remember was that every Marine is supposed to be a marksman. Musketry is the backbone of the Marine Corps. And the rifle range is the big deal in boot camp, and I am a left-handed person totally. I can't do anything right-handed. So the time came to fire, and I get down in the left-handed position -- and we used to wear something called a pith helmet. And whack, I'm hit on top of the pith helmet with a swagger stick by one of the drill instructors, who said, "We don't have wrong-handed people in the Marine Corps." And he said, "You're going to have to learn to shoot right-handed, son." And I just couldn't. The reason for that is that with the old M1 Garand rifle, when the shell casing would eject, it would come right across my vision, line of vision. That didn't bother me at all, but it bothered them. But finally a sergeant at the rifle range who happened to be from LA, from Hollywood, he had been in the movie business, and he was kind of sympathetic to me. He said, "Let the kid shoot the way he wants to shoot."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Shoot the way you want to shoot?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Clock chiming.) That's all right.

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: So at any rate, I got permission to shoot left-handed, and I qualified at the rifle range, and I became a left-handed Marine marksman.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Phone beeping off the hook.) It's going to do that for a couple of seconds. Did many guys wash out of boot camp?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Not many. Some did for emotional reasons, for illness, just breakdowns, either physical or emotional, but not many, not many.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not many couldn't hack it because of the dehumanizing training, huh?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: They saw to it that you did hack it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They wouldn't let them wash out, would they?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else interesting happen during your training?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: When boot camp was over, all right, we -- shall I go into that?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. (Phone beeping off the hook.) I wonder if we should -- (Phone stops beeping off the hook.) All right. Did you guys get a chance to have much of a break during boot camp? Did you get to --

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- do anything for fun?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: No. The call was, When I say fall in, I want to see a cloud of dust, and when that dust settles, I want to see 63 balls of blank at rigid attention, and that was it. You -- just complete response day and night. There was no -- no, there were no breaks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No chance to go into town or do anything?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you assigned an outfit at that point?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: No, you're assigned to training platoons in boot camp, and when the eight or ten weeks, whatever it was, was over, then you were assigned to a unit for advanced training, which was generally, in those days, maybe six weeks, and then it was aboard ship and overseas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. So when did you ship overseas?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: I had six weeks of training at a place called San Mateo barracks, which was located right next to Victor McLaughlin's estate. Remember the actor --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: -- Victor McLaughlin? He had an estate, and he allowed us to practice landing maneuvers on his beach. So we would come ashore on Higgins boats and charge the beach and up toward Victor McLaughlin's house.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: But that's where I got my advanced training as a forward observer for artillery, and then after six weeks found myself on a troop ship, and it was just jammed with guys. We roamed around -- seemed like we were roaming around the Pacific. It was 51 days aboard ship, mostly standing in an endless chow line. You'd get up in the morning, get in this line, eventually get to the gally where you were fed and get into another line for the next meal, and there were card games in the chow line and every other activity you can think of. But then one morning we woke up. We were at anchor, woke up, and as far as I could see, there were ships at anchor. We were at a place called Ulithi, and we were just amassing troops. And at that point I was assigned to an outfit. I was assigned to the 3rd Marine Division, and they were getting organized for the assault on Guam. Saipan had already been hit by another Marine division, and if you make -- if you remember Saipan, there were tremendous casualties there. Guam didn't get as much publicity as Saipan did. They were both in the Mariana Islands, but Guam was equally bloody and lasted a lot longer because it was never really secured. There was so much jungle there that we were constantly patrolling for Japanese stragglers, and you may remember that -- oh, God, I think it was in the '50's or '60's -- two Japanese soldiers came out of the jungle, finally surrendering, thinking that the war was still on. So that's how dense the jungle was on Guam. But at any rate, at Ulithi I was assigned to the 3rd Division, boarded ship and participated in the invasion of Guam.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When was that invasion performed?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: June of 1944.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How early did you hit the beach in that invasion, first wave?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, essentially. It's hard to depict waves, but yeah, it was the first day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So describe that. Describe loading on the landing craft and hitting the beach.

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Going over the side of a troop ship on a what is known as a Jacob's ladder is a very harrowing experience. It's just a rope ladder, you know, and you've got your rifle and your pack and then somebody above you stepping on your fingers as you work your way down, and the Higgins boat, the landing craft, is bobbing up and down in the swell alongside the ship like a cork, and it's a very small-looking thing as you go down this ladder. And when you were ready to let go of the ladder and jump into that boat, you better time it just right or you're apt to fall between the Higgins boat and the ship, and that happened to quite -- not to quite a few, but many, many guys slipped. There were accidents. Jump into Higgins boat. You're jam packed there. You really can't see over the gunnels, and errrrrr, you're roaring toward shore, and suddenly you grind up on the sand, and the ramp drops and the guy yells, "Get out." The coxswain of the landing craft wants to back that thing out of there and leave as quickly as he can, so he wants the Marines off. So off we went into the sand and scurried around until the officers got us organized, and we started proceeding inland into the jungle.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have much resistance when you hit the beach?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah, there was a lot of mortar fire. The Japs always had the mortar zeroed in on the beach, a lot of machine gunfire, and there were a lot of casualties on the beach, and that's why they wanted us off the beach and into covers as soon as we could.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were you thinking and feeling the first time you were under fire there?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Strangely enough, when you're 17, not that you don't have any fear, you think that nothing can happen to you or your mother will raise hell. You know, it's strange, but I did not have any fear at that moment, at that point in time, and so I scurried back, and I was excited. I mean, it was like watching a movie. It was almost like an out-of-body experience, if you will. I was watching this young guy, saying, "Hey, you finally joined the Marines, and here you are in a battle just like" -- what was it that I saw before I enlisted -- "Guadalcanal Diary." And I remember seeing it saying, "Wow, like to be one of those guys." So suddenly I was one of those guys. And after that the excitement wore off and the misery of trying to survive in that jungle took over. And it was hot on Guam, mosquito-ridden, malaria-ridden, muddy. You were never dry, and the mosquitos never stopped biting you. And we came down with a variation of malaria called Dengue Fever, D-E-N-G-U-E, and when guys came down with that, they were just racked with bone-breaking pain. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get Dengue Fever?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yes, I had Dengue several times, and it was -- it was a very miserable thing. Guam was, quote, secured. That's the Marine term for it. We got to high ground, we got -- there's no organized resistance, etcetera, in 31 days. But, you know, that's a myth. That's a fallacy. We were competing with the division on Saipan for who could secure the island faster. But then we settled into areas, and the real war began. We would have patrol activity daily. We'd send platoons out, companies into the jungle chasing down these stragglers, and there were thousands of them that just drifted back into the jungle. And that was very hard duty, very hard duty, and it went on day in and day out for months and months and months.

One of the problems on Guam was that there were no -- we hadn't had any fresh food for the longest time, just rations, and guys didn't want to eat. It was -- you know, you'd just get tired of that food. Have a little story about a character that I met. He was an old-time China Marine, as they were called. These were guys that had served in China on the gunboats in the '30's, and they all were allowed to wear a special kind of headgear. It was like a Smokey the Bear hat, only it had a special crush to it.

This guy's name was Kelly, and I noticed a tattoo that he had on his arm. Now, the traditional Marine Corps tattoo was "Death Before Dishonor," and everybody wanted to have one of those things. Kelly was an iconoclast. He had a tattoo that said "Dishonor Before Death," and he thought it was funny, and every outfit that he went into had an officer who didn't think it was funny. So he was constantly being broken from sergeant to private, but he had many years in the Marine Corps.

When we finally got some fresh food, it came from New Zealand. We got this fresh food from New Zealand, and it consisted of mutton and big chunks of rutabaga. So the word spread, "Hey, we've got fresh meat, we've got fresh vegetables," and everybody was all excited, and we went into this mess hall, and hot in that mess hall and again the line, and we had to eat standing up to expedite coming through.

And our, quote, cook didn't really have a good feel for cooking mutton because it would -- there were big chunks of sheep with lanolin still on it, coated, in other words, grease. And Kelly took one look at it. They had heaped it up in his mess kit, and he said, "I can't eat this." And I said, "I can." And he looked at me in surprise, and he dumped it in my mess kit, and I just consumed it. I was a growing boy, and I had a voracious appetite, and I ate the mutton and the rutabagas. And at that point, Kelly made a pronouncement. He said, "Kid, you are a survivor." He says, "You're gonna make it. I guarantee it." And that was kind of prophetic because it turned out I did, fortunately, make it.

So that became the routine on Guam: Patrols every day, boredom, inspections. There's an old song, The Raggedy Ass Marines Are on Parade. We barely had clothes that were in one piece. It was hard, you know, to supply us at that point, and our dungarees were kind of shabby and so forth, but still we had to fall out for our parades.

A side anecdote: I wandered off down a trail. The Guamanians, who were known as Chamorro -- that was their racial stock, Polynesian stock -- used water buffalo as their means of transportation, little carts. And I followed one of these trails, just exploring, and I came to a clearing in the jungle, and there on stilts was a little hut with palm froms for the roof, and underneath the floor, elevated floor, were some mangy-looking chickens and a little pig and a whole -- an entire family, mostly women, just women.

Their name was Manabooson (ph.) And at first they were frightened to see me, but we became friends. There were three young women there and an old grandmother who chewed beetle nuts, so her gums were constantly red, but it kept her going, kept her mellow, and she kept an eye on me to see that I didn't get too close to the young daughters. But they were very friendly and very nice. And soon I started bringing them leftovers from the mess tent.

Powdered eggs. Nobody would eat these powdered scrambled eggs, and I'd bring back just cans of it for them and anything else I could scrounge up. I found some old -- we call them boondockers, high-top shoes that we wore, and I brought them for the girls, and they loved them. They wore these high-top Marine shoes. And I kept the family fed, and they were very grateful to me, and they asked if I would like my laundry done.

Well, all of us had one or two sets of khakis that we would wear for these inspections, and I would take my khakis to them, and they would wash them and iron them using coconut milk as the starch, and I would show up for inspections in the starched khakis. And we had a sergeant major who was a career Marine, and he took me aside, and he said, "Listen, you little SOB. Where are you getting your clothes done? You're making everybody look bad." And I never revealed the source. And he threatened me with everything, but I was the sharpest-looking Marine on Guam for the longest time by virtue my relationship with the Manaboosons.

Anyhow, that routine took place on Guam for many months, and then in February of 1945, we got the word that we were going on a campaign. Most everybody assumed that it was Iwo Jima because we kept hearing broadcasts that the Navy planes were bombing this little island; and when we got aboard ship, on deck, the officers briefed us. They had a map of this little island that was shaped like a pork chop, two-by-four, two miles by four miles, and he said, "Here's this volcano, extinct volcano, Suribachi, at this end," and they told us it was Iwo Jima and that the Navy had been bombing it for 102 straight days. "Hopefully the resistance would be neutralized, but don't count on it," which was good advice.

There were three Marine divisions assigned to this campaign, the 3rd, 4th and 5th Divisions. We were amazed to hear that there was a 5th Marine Division because usually Marines didn't have that many divisions, but there was a 5th Division, and they were kind of new. The 3rd Division, my outfit, was under the command of a general by the name of Graves B. Erskine. Naturally, the guys did a lot with that name. Graves B., yeah, there will be graves. And he was a favorite of the overall commander of the operation of that fleet Marine force, it was called, and we were given the center part of the island as our thrust because the 3rd Division had a pretty good reputation.

My recollection of that landing is still fairly poignant, and I remember that at three a.m. we were awakened, told to saddle up with all our gear on and report to different positions on deck, where we would disembark different landing nets. I remember wandering down to the head, the bathroom, for one last visit before, and it was strangely deserted and quiet below deck. And I remember going up, finding my position along the rail, getting ready to disembark, and it was dark, and words kept coming over the loud speaker system, this and that, and it took on a more tense -- a --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So the words were coming over the loud speaker?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah, and this was a little bit more intimidating than Guam had been. And I remember going over the side, going down that Jacob's ladder and trying to spot that Higgins boat bobbing up and down, jumping as the Higgins boat came up luckily. And we were all in there very quiet, and there was a lot after water and oil sloshing around the bottom of the boat.

And there was this guy that we called Pappy because he was all of 32 years old, and he was kind of a portly guy, and he was rather tense, and he used to call me Fox Man. He said, "Hey, Fox Man, do me a favor." He said, "The strap on my legging is loose, and I don't want to trip," he said, "and I can't bend over." So I carried a weapon that was known as -- that is known as a BAR, Browning automatic rifle. How I was saddled with that, I don't know, but the thing weighed more than I did. I weighed 145 pounds in those days, and the ammunition belt and that weapon weighed more than I did. But at any rate, I gave him the weapon to hold, and I knelt down in that cold, oily water and fastened his bootstrap for him. And he was very grateful. He thanked me. He never -- he never saw his 33rd birthday. He was killed.

And we sustained, as you may know, very, very heavy casualties on Iwo Jima. But, you know, some live and some die, and you can't figure out why and how. A Congressional Medal of Honor winner by the name of -- Marines always had picturesque names. This guy's name was Manilla John Basilone. Why Manilla John, I don't know. He was from New Jersey. But he had -- he won a Congressional Medal on Guadalcanal, and he was sent home, and he could have toured on bond drives for the rest of the war, and he chose to come back for this thing. And standing on the beach, he was killed by a mortar fragment the very first day.

There were two ships that anchored the line of debark -- debarkation, and all the Higgins boats circled until these boats dropped their pennants, and that was the signal for the boats to go toward the beach, and they all formed a line, and we went onto the beach. And when we disembarked, immediately the Japanese on Mount Suribachi had mortars, small, five-inch field pieces, heavy machine guns, all zeroed in on the beaches.

Each division had a different beach, a section of the beach, and we were all assigned different movements. The 5th Division was to go up the beach straight north; the 4th Division was to go across the island, which was two miles, and then go up the other beach; and the 3rd Division, mine, was just to go inland a little bit and then go up the center. Well, the best laid plans, etcetera, etcetera. It became chaotic because when we hit that beach, it was deep black volcanic sand. It was like being on the surface of the moon literally. There was no vegetation, and guys just couldn't move. They -- they got bogged down. The vessels, the tanks, trucks, half-tracks got bogged down. They were there every which way, different angles, just askew.

And casualties, bodies all over, screams for corpsmen, Navy corpsmen. Those were the medics. "Corpsmen, corpsmen." A lot of screaming, a lot of chaos, a lot of smoke, a lot of smell. And this was a nightmare. This was a nightmare. The beach master, plural, beach masters, these were the men with the bullhorns who were assigned the job of getting some order on the beach, and they were bellowing orders, Do this and do that. One of the orders was "Pull those bodies out of the way," so that we could lay mats -- metal mats down to get these vehicles ashore. And so it was like stacking cordwood, just throwing the bodies out of the way.

It was as if they were not human, and soon the vehicles were able to get some traction and to move over this first ridge where the ground was somewhat firmer, and they could move. It was inch by inch that first day, crawling. Now, the majority of my division didn't come ashore the first day. I came ashore the first day because I was a forward observer, and I was there with a small group. I had become a corporal by that time, which was a big deal in the Marines. You usually had to sign up for another four-year hitch to become a PFC, but because I could do this geometry in my head, they made me kind of a little section leader.

So we inched our way up little by little, and soon there was some order, and we found where we had to be and started moving up the island. Now, the Japanese had dug in on this island for 20-some years, and they had 20 to 30 thousand very elite Japanese Marines of -- special troops. And they had tunneled this island so completely that we could be walking up a slight incline, and it was like somebody opened a slot in a door. The ground -- the incline that we were -- the ground opened up, and a Japanese machine gun known as the Namboo (ph.) would stick its nose out, spray the (?)cowm(?), withdraw, close the little slot and disappear. Guys would run over to where the slot was, punch it open, throw grenades in there, call for a flamethrower, but they were long gone. They could pop up behind us, take the tunnel, pop up behind us. And this went on for days.

In the meantime, a couple of companies were sent up Suribachi, and everybody knows that story. They worked their way up there. When they got to the top -- and Joe Rosenthal kind of staged that flag-waving to make sure that they had the right size flag, because the first one that went up was a little flag, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you see either one of those raisings?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, I was not far. I mean, it was very visible from where we were. But when that flag went up, there were literally hundreds of ships off the beach there, and everybody hit their horn, you know, and it just -- it just was an experience hard to explain, but everybody froze where they were, and you could feel the goose bumps, you know. The Secretary of the Navy at that time was, I think, Forestal, and he happened to be there on the beach, and he said to one of the generals that -- it was another picturesque Marine name, Holland M. Smith. And naturally, that became Howling Mad Smith. But Forestal told Howling Mad at that moment when the flag went up and the horns were blaring that he said that this guarantees that there will be a Marine Corps 500 years from now.

He said, "This is the most historic moment in the history of warfare," etcetera, etcetera, and he was quite moved. But that was just the beginning of things. We started moving up the island foot by foot, yard by yard. Every Marine division has three infantry regiments and one artillery regiment in it. The 3rd Marine Division had the 12th Marines, which was artillery. We fired 105 millimeter Howitzers. And then there was the 3rd, 9th and 21st Marines, and they were the infantry regiments. I was assigned to the 21st Marines as an observer, and I would travel with their skirmish line.

My job was to call "fire" from the guns to support this skirmish line and make sure that our shells were landing where they should. The Marines had utilized and thought they perfected something called a rolling barrage, and that was a very touchy kind of a thing, where we would drop a line of shells maybe a hundred yards at the most in front of an advancing skirmish line of infantry, and the trick was to keep raising the elevation so that the shells kept dropping in front so that there would be a wall of artillery explosions. Sometimes shells could drop short for various reasons. The powder might be wet; instead of seven bags of powder, we loaded six in the excitement. It didn't happen often, but when it did, the artillery was referred to as Murder, Incorporated. The Marines had black humor always.

In my forward observer team, there was a lieutenant and an NCO, me. We each had a group of -- and we observed. We had Navajos, code talkers. We would string wire and call back information, and if it needed to be coded, the Navajos would do it. I dreaded having to call fire for a rolling barrage. The lieutenant, who was kind of an aristocrat from the Mainline of Philadelphia, Lieutenant Wilhelm Paddy (ph.) -- I'll never forget his name, and he had a head that was like a bowling ball with reddish-blond hair cut very short, and he used to challenge anybody in the outfit to butt heads with him, you know. He was a character, but he called the first rolling barrage.

Subsequently, toward the end, when we got into the early part of March, I called one very nervously, but fortunately, I didn't drop any shells on the troops. We, as a forward observing team, were responsible for our own security. That's why I carried a Browning automatic rifle. I would have to be there with binoculars. We'd set up the automatic weapon, we'd put a little perimeter around ourselves, and then we'd have to pick up and move with the infantry. So it was very nervous work. I was up there with the 21st for about 18 days.

Then they gave me a break, pulled us off. And he said, "Now you get a couple of days of rest." And their idea of rest was to put us on a burial detail. There were bodies. Marine bodies were pulled back and put into covers. The Japanese bodies were laying there in the sun. They were rotting. There was fear of pestilence. I remember getting ready to bury some Japanese dead, and somebody said, "Look up this way, son," and on a hill behind me was a photographer from Leatherneck Magazine, and he took a shot of me on that burial detail.

I'm going to digress a little bit here. Carl Reese, who was a radio personality, still on the air here in Cleveland, was very much interested in Marine Corps lore and history, and he found a book called Uncommon Valor: The History of the Marines on Iwo Jima. I still have a copy of it. And he found that picture of me that the Leatherneck Magazine photographer took while we were on that burial detail, but it -- that raised hackles on the back of my neck when I saw it 40 years later.

One Japanese who had died on his hands and knees with his head buried in the sand, his hips elevated, and his tunic had slid down his back, and the sun was bearing down on the middle of his back, and it raised a huge blister. And one of the guys that was with me -- and I refer to him as an idiot. I said, "Don't touch that," but he grabbed this corpse by the back of the tunic and pulled him over backwards, and that blister broke, and a smell emanated from that thing that I cannot to this day describe; but we had to handle that corpse and get it in the ground.

And for days afterwards, I kept washing my hands, trying to get that smell off. Well, the smell wasn't on my hands. It was in my nose, in the olfactory nerves or cells of my nose, and it stayed there for days, and I couldn't eat anything because of that smell. It felt like anything I was eating was dead flesh.

But that was our rest, the burial detail. When we went back up on the line -- I think it was March 8 -- the biggest artillery barrage in the history of the Marine Corps took place, because we were coming to the final concentration of Japanese strength at the northern end of the island. And the commander of the island had his bunker there, and we just tried our best to blow everything apart.

Well, I called fire for that thing, and finally the infantry got to the very northern end of the island. There were shear cliffs there. A lot of civilians who had been living -- Japanese civilians who had been living on Iwo Jima chose to jump over those cliffs to the rocks below rather than surrender; although many Japanese soldiers did, not many, but some surrendered at that point, came out of their caves. Some of the Marines scaled down that cliff, got to the ocean, filled some five-gallon gasoline cans with water and sent it to the commanding general, saying "Water from the northern end of the island. We're here. We've secured the island, but this is not for consumption."

And that was essentially the campaign. It went from the 23rd of February, I believe -- we left the island about the 20th of March and headed back to Guam, went through a heavy, heavy typhoon, and that was an experience. We were not sure that the troop ships could survive that, but they did. Got back to Guam and immediately started training again and found out that we were going to be the spearhead division for the invasion of Kyushu, southernmost island of Japan.

And so we were training with specific tactics, which would have been, of course, futile and etcetera, and did that until one day a guy came running through the tent area yelling, "Hey, they dropped the magic bomb! The war is over!" "What?" We figured he was drunk on the native drink, fermented coconut juice, that we used to drink called tuba, which is a poisonous beverage. But he was celebrating.

They had dropped the bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the war was over. And I said, "Well, I'm going to go home now." I had been overseas almost 24 months. And for some perverse reason -- I don't know why -- my orders got mixed up or what, but I had a lot of -- you know, we had points, so much for a campaign, so much for every month overseas. I had more than enough points to be going home with troops that were already being rotated home, but I wasn't going home for some reason. And one day we were outfitted with heavy fur jackets, fur-lined mittens and big, heavy hat, and we were going to be sent to China, to Chen Sin (ph.), and we were going to be guards on trains carrying all sorts of -- gold, whatever else on the mainland of China.

And here I had had Dengue fever and malaria, both eight times. My blood was so watery thin from all those months in the tropics, and I probably didn't weigh 140 pounds then. And I was relieved, tired.

My youthful ebullience by this time had worn off, and I was anxious to be heading home. And we fell out for inspection, naturally, and -- I'm trying to think of -- I don't recall the name of the -- it was a general and a sergeant major, and they were coming down the ranks, looking us over, telling us that we had an important job to do in China. And for some reason this general saw my dog tags, and he could tell by the number. He said, "Son, how long have you been over here?" And I said, "Twenty-three months." And he bellowed, "Sergeant major!" and he said, "Get this man's name, and," he said, "get him home."

He said, "Son, take that gear off. You're not going to China." And I don't know, it was just a miracle. I didn't go to China. I gave them back their fur-lined gear and was aboard a troop ship on my way to San Francisco, and shortly thereafter sent home on 30-day leave, and then sent to Bainbridge, Maryland, where I was discharged.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you did get home after two years?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: I had had a dog since I was in elementary school, and the dog went all through my schooling with me and survived the war. And the parents of -- I think Jack Clyman (ph.) mentioned that this group of guys that hung out together had a club, and our parents continued the club while we were in the service.

Well, all these parents had gathered at my home for my homecoming, and the main -- the high point of my homecoming was to see how my dog, Blackie, would react when he saw me. And the dog came up to me and smelled, and at first he didn't -- he was getting old. He didn't realize it was me, but then it dawned on him.

He recognized the smell, and the hair on his back just stood straight up, and he started jumping hysterically, wouldn't stop. And everybody just wept at that, watching that dog. But that was my -- that was my homecoming, and it was hard. I was planning to go on to college, you know, on the GI Bill, and I was going to get a chance to go to college, which would not have happened were it not for the GI Bill.

And I was just in many ways almost too old emotionally to be thinking about going to college, and it was a hard adjustment. It was a hard adjustment. Eleanor Roosevelt had visited some Marines overseas, and she made her famous statement that -- and she meant well, but she said, "But these Marines are going to need to be recivilized for a long time before they can go back into normal society," which was in many ways true, maybe not to the extent that it was misinterpreted, but it took a long while to readjust.

One of the wonderful things was to be able to sleep with no clothes on and not be swatting mosquitos. I mean, what a blessing to be free at last of mosquitos. Sometimes Marine Corps swear words would pop out inadvertently. Everybody had one episode like that where you'd talked to your mother and say, Pass the blanking butter, you know. And that happened, you know, and I -- mortified, but it was so instinctive. You were 23 months overseas. It's a long time in those days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies over there, overseas?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yes, I had one -- I called him a lunatic. He was from a very well-to-do family in Connecticut. He had gone to Yale, and he could have been an officer, but he enlisted and he used to yell, for no apparent reason, "For God, for country, for Yale," you know, and guys would just look at him like he was a nut, but that was his thing. But he invited me to his society wedding, sent me a fancy invitation, and I had to scurry around to get enough money for air fare and to get a proper suit and so forth to go to this wedding in Connecticut, which I did do.

And we stayed in touch for many, many years. And there were a couple of fellows from Cleveland, Jimmy Dockerty (ph.) and Lenny Leone (ph.) The three of us hung out together during our training days, but eventually lost track of them. When The Plain Dealer did a story on me -- I think it was the 50th or some anniversary of the invasion of Iwo Jima. They did a story on me. I heard from people -- Marines I didn't know all over the country, calling me up on the phone, you know, and talked. Some of them apparently very lonely.

Now we're all old men when this is taking place, you know. Only one guy from my outfit called me. He said, "I'm still kicking. I'm still" -- he was Polish. He said, "Remember me? I'm the beanpole they used to call the Pollock." I said, "Yes." He said, "I'm still here. I retired from the Public Steel," I think it was, "still kicking." He said, "I'm glad to hear you are," you know, and that's about it.

But a guy -- a reporter called me from Florida, West Palm, and he wanted to interview me on the phone. I said, "What possible interest can I be to people in West Palm? Why would you want to interview me?" He said, "Son" -- well, not son. "Sir," he said, "there aren't many of you guys left. You don't realize this." He said, "You're a precious commodity, so yeah, I want to ask you some questions by readers."

And when I made my presentation at the Cleveland County Library System, there were a lot of young college and high school types in the audience, and when I was through with my story, about a half a dozen came up with books on Iwo Jima that they had purchased, and they wanted me to autograph the book.

I was just stunned. I said, "Why would you want my autograph? I'm a corporal. I'm not" -- you know. And they said, "No, you don't understand." They said, "You're an important commodity that you're still around, and we want to show you some respect." I was very touched by it. I could not believe it. But anyhow --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies over there in Guam or Iwo Jima?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Oh, yeah. My outfit had 130 percent casualties, in other words, 30 percent of the replacements. They were sending cooks and bakers. Now, everybody in the Marine Corps theoretically is a marksman, but here came these cooks and bakers, who hadn't fired their weapon in a long time, as replacements. No, we lost many, many guys, many guys. One guy in particular who had been a sports hero of mine, Niles Kinnick, was an All American at Iowa. When I was watching, listening to sports in my high school days, Niles Kinnick in Iowa, I remember every exploit of his. He had the same job that I did. He was a forward observer. He was an officer, and his position was overrun in a banzai attack, and he was killed. But yeah, everybody, many, many people that I knew were killed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of mail call, getting anything interesting from home?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah, I got my diploma on Guam. I didn't have to take the final exam in trigonometry. The principal wrote me a very nice letter, saying that the school owed me a debt of gratitude, and I sure deserved my diploma. And then, of course, those much-treasured SWAK lipstick smudges.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did you get a lot of those?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah, sure. The girls were very -- very generous with the letters.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: These were high school classmates?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, and I had one special girl. I guess you'd call her a sweetheart, and she was absolutely certain that when I returned, we would be getting married; but fortunately or unfortunately, I had an older sister, and she interceded. My mother thought that this young woman was just perfect, and this girl lived at our house for periods of time when I was overseas.

And my sister, I remember, confronted my mother. She said, "He's 19 years old." She said, "What are you doing, getting him married off? Let him live his life." So fortunately I did not get married, which would have been a disaster, I think, at that point in time, although many of my contemporaries, these fellows that were a year ahead of me at Glenville High School, in short order, they were getting married and settling down and, you know, going on to college.

And my life didn't quite go that way. I was interested in many things, and finally my career in advertising and film-making started, and that occupied me, and I didn't get married until much later in life. I was in my 30's when I finally got married, when I was finally ready to get married; put it that way. I seemed to have a lot of wild oats to sow.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Of course as far as mail call, you would get those great newsletters from the parents group, right?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Oh, yes, yeah. Yeah, those came through with great regularity. And one of the parents was very fine writer. I believe it was a man named Victor Berg, and he wrote a beautiful newsletter. And yes, that was very welcomed because the names and images of home were getting increasingly vague. I had a hard time visualizing what people looked like and what they said. My world was, you know, Guam, Marine Corps, and this was a link with society and civilization and sanity in a way. Yeah, so those newsletters were very welcomed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: These newsletters were put together by parents of how many guys that were hanging around together?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: I think there were 13 or 14 of us. They were all very special guys. They were all a year older than I was, but they were all student athletes. They were the cream of the crop at our high school, and I was very, very flattered to be invited to pledge this club, but I had a year of membership before we all broke up and went to the service. So it was such a closely knit group that the parents came together and formed a club. Our name was kind of a contraction of three names, All Good Men, and it became Algomen, and that was the name of the club. And the parents formed the Algomen Parents Club, and they stayed together for many, many years. Even after the war and we came back, they had their Saturday night card games and whatever else. So yes, it was a very unusual and unique group.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And just so people know, the newsletters contained news about all these different guys, and each kid would get a copy and know what their buddies were doing?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Yes, yeah. And again, everybody was in active service, you know, in every theater, and it was interesting to hear that this guy was there. And many of them -- many of the guys managed to hook up in France and the Hawaiian Islands and so forth. I -- let me digress back to Iwo Jima. I hooked up inadvertently with one guy who is still with us, still living. His name is Howard Orputt (ph.), Howie Orputt.

He was the only member of that group that was my age. He was a year younger. And he went into the service, into the Marines, a year after I did, and he was in that 5th Division, the newly formed 5th, and I didn't know that. And I was dug in. We had a little foxhole during a rest period on Iwo Jima with this Warrenthol (ph.), this guy from Yale, and we were in this deep foxhole, and we had a cover on it, and suddenly the shelter cover was pulled back, and this face leans in, and slant-eyes, a scraggly beard. And we thought, My God, we're overrun by Japanese.

Well, it was Howie Orputt, and he does have slanty eyes. And in that quick moment, we took him for Japanese. He was in the 5th Division. He knew from this newsletter that I was on the island in the 3rd Division, and he worked his way through all that debris and activity to my outfit, found me, and we had a nice visit. And the next day I went back to -- I said I'd come over and visit him. He was in the 25th Marines -- 25th regiment. And I snuck away from where we were bivouacked. We were on a rest break. And I remember going across this airfield, Motiyami Airfield No. 2, and there was a CB, construction battalion.

They were all older guys, and they kind of adopted the Marines as their kid brothers. One guy had a bulldozer there, and he said, "Where are you going?" I said, "To get to the other side." He said, "Wait a minute. I'm going to walk you across." He raised his blade and said, "Stay behind the blade," took me across the airfield, and I found -- eventually found the 25st Marines dug in. And I remember saying to one guy, a very haggard-looking sergeant -- I said, "You know where the 25th Marines are?"

And he looked at -- spit some tobacco. He says, "Yeah, you'll find them at Hollywood and Vine." And I asked my friend, "What's the significance of that?" He said, "Well, we had a reputation of being Hollywood Marines." That was what they were called, Hollywood Marines. So naturally they would be at Hollywood and Vine.

But anyhow, I found Howie, had a visit with him, worked my way back to my outfit, got chewed out for being gone and exposing myself to some danger trying to visit a buddy. You know, they said, "This ain't high school." But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did they get the reputation as Hollywood Marines, bunch of pretty boys?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: It was a newly formed division, and yeah, they spent a lot of time on liberty in LA, and naturally, Hollywood and Vine, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very good. Do you think that covers it? Anything else?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: I think that's --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: We've covered everything in the presentation?

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: Pretty much so, pretty much so.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I still have tape if there's anything you want to add.

sp.speaker: Aaron S. Fox
sp.p: No, I think that we've got the essence of it.
